title: Dynamic Archetypal Coordination: Separating Common, System-Specific and History-Dependent Effects on Behavioral Selection
content: An animal expresses one behavioral system at a time, and the rules that decide which system gains the body act over seconds, hours and days. Dynamic Archetypal Coordination (DAC) is proposed here as a circuit-level hypothesis about how conserved behavioral systems trade access to the body. A comparator with a no-action option sorts manipulations by two measurements: a term common to all systems changes the frequency of no action and leaves the ratio between active behaviors fixed, whereas a system-specific term changes that ratio. Three update rules, READ, WRITE and SWITCH, specify how an executed act changes the terms of the next decision; each is written as an explicit update and located at identified neurons in Drosophila melanogaster and in mice or rats. Circuit data show that competing systems are coordinated in three ways within overlapping hypothalamic or protocerebral nuclei: graded activity of the same cells, largely separate subpopulations and directed inhibition between populations. In each case the architecture persists and access changes. Sleep pressure is evaluated as the leading candidate for a common term. Current data show a general rise in arousal threshold together with system-specific effects, so the coupling of sleep to each system becomes a quantity to measure. Durable writing of contest outcomes occurs under identified conditions of repetition, hormonal state and post-experience sleep. Extension to the remaining systems of the Systema Behavorum is outlined as future work. Every statement carries an evidence tag, and each claim is paired with a discriminating experiment.
